opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me, Peter. Honestly, I'd say we've made a lot of progress and very little progress at the same time, and both are true.

On one side, we're much better at what you might call the "easy problems." We can put electrodes in people's brains, which is part of what I've done with patients undergoing neurosurgery, and watch individual neurons respond to a face, a concept, a memory. We can sometimes see a decision forming in the brain before the person reports making it. We can tell, with decent accuracy, whether a patient who looks unresponsive is actually aware. That's real progress, and twenty or thirty years ago it would have sounded like science fiction.

But the hard question, why any of that activity *feels* like something, why there's an experience of being you rather than just a very complicated machine processing information, we haven't cracked. We have competing theories. Some say consciousness is about how integrated information is in a system. Others say it's about information being broadcast widely across the brain. Others tie it to prediction. And the uncomfortable truth is that when people have designed experiments to pit these theories against each other, the results haven't cleanly crowned a winner.

Part of the problem is that consciousness is the one thing we can't observe from the outside. I can measure your neurons, but I only know you're conscious because you tell me, and because you're built like me. That works for humans. It gets very shaky with animals, with patients in comas, and now with AI systems that can *say* they're conscious very convincingly.

So my honest assessment: we've gone from philosophy to having real data and testable theories, which is a big step. But we're still a bit like early astronomers who can track the planets precisely without yet understanding gravity. We know a lot about the *correlates*. We don't yet know the *cause*.

fable-5.1.text:
So, I'd say we've made enormous progress on everything around consciousness, and almost no progress on consciousness itself. That sounds like a cop-out, but let me explain what I mean.

If you'd asked a neuroscientist thirty years ago, "where in the brain does the decision happen, where does the memory get stored, what happens when you see a face," they'd have given you a vague answer. Today I can put a person in a scanner, or in my case put electrodes directly inside the brain of patients who are undergoing surgery, and I can tell you with surprising accuracy what they're thinking about, what they're about to choose before they know it, whether they're dreaming, whether they're lying. We can decode the content. We've gotten very good at the "what."

What we haven't touched is the "why does it feel like anything." Why is there an experience attached to all this processing? Philosophers call it the hard problem, and honestly, I think a lot of neuroscientists quietly decided to just not work on it, because you can't get a grant for it, you can't publish a clean paper on it. So the field split. There are the people who study the neural correlates, meaning what lights up when you're conscious of something versus when you're not, and that work is excellent. And then there are a handful of theories, global workspace, integrated information theory, higher-order theories, that try to say what consciousness actually is. And those theories, I'd say, are still at the stage where smart people disagree and no experiment has really killed any of them.

Actually, there was this big adversarial collaboration a few years ago where they tried to pit two of the leading theories against each other with pre-registered predictions, and the result was basically that both theories got some things wrong and nobody conceded. Which tells you something about the state of the field.

The thing I find interesting, and maybe a bit humbling, is that the most honest progress has come from narrowing the question. Instead of "what is consciousness," you ask "what's the difference in the brain between a patient in a coma who will wake up and one who won't," or "what's happening when an anesthetic switches you off." Those questions have answers, and they matter for real people. So my assessment is: we're like astronomers before we understood gravity. We can map the sky beautifully. We just don't yet know what's holding it all together.

astra-6.text:
I think we’ve made a lot of progress in studying the brain, but we have to be careful about equating that with understanding consciousness. We can increasingly identify what changes in the brain when someone falls asleep, wakes up, or becomes aware of something. That gives us clues about the conditions that support conscious experience.

The harder question is why any of that activity feels like something from the inside. Why does processing information about a color produce the experience of seeing red? Measuring the activity and explaining the experience are different achievements.

So I’d say we’re making progress on questions we can define and test. But we don’t yet have an agreed explanation of consciousness, or even complete agreement on what would count as one. That’s a substantial limitation, but it also makes this a fascinating scientific problem.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’ve made a lot of progress in studying the things around consciousness, but we still don’t have an agreed explanation of consciousness itself. We can study what changes in the brain when you fall asleep, when you’re anesthetized, or when something enters your awareness. We can identify activity that tracks those changes. That’s real progress.

But there’s a difference between identifying the brain activity associated with an experience and explaining why that activity feels like something. Why does seeing red have a subjective quality at all? We don’t yet have a clear answer to that.

Part of the difficulty is measurement. In most science, you can observe the thing you’re trying to explain. With consciousness, I have access to my own experience, but I don’t have direct access to yours. I can ask you about it, and I can measure your brain, but connecting those two is precisely the problem we’re trying to solve.

So I’m optimistic about the experiments, and more cautious about claims that we’ve solved the mystery.
